MoA-Structured Decode Attention
DNF Derivation, KV-Cache Accumulation, GQA/MQA, and OpenACC Kernel

Lenore Mullin1,∗ 1University at Albany, SUNY lmullin@albany.edu *Corresponding author and Gaétan Hains2 2LACL, Université Paris-Est Créteil gaetan.hains@u-pec.fr
June 2026
Abstract

We derive four memory-optimal inference artifacts for transformer attention using the Mathematics of Arrays (MoA), each following directly from the forward-pass Denotational Normal Form (DNF) of [1] with the query-row index fixed to the current decode step. The artifacts are: (1) a single-query decode DNF in which the ψ\psi-reduction eliminates the K⊤K^{\top} buffer algebraically, achieving (dk+n​dk+n​dv+dv)×4​B(d_{k}+nd_{k}+nd_{v}+d_{v})\times 4\,\mathrm{B} Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM) traffic (Storage Theorem 2.7 of [1]), result numerically verified to ‖err‖∞≤2×10−7\|\mathrm{err}\|_{\infty}\leq 2\times 10^{-7}; (2) a C/OpenACC Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) kernel with Operational Normal Form (ONF) stride arithmetic and hardware-coalesced memory access, verified to ‖err‖∞=0\|\mathrm{err}\|_{\infty}=0 (exact IEEE-754 floating-point arithmetic); (3) a multi-step KV-cache with O⁡(dk+dv)O(d_{k}+d_{v}) per-step append via MoA concatenation #\#; and (4) Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and Multi-Query Attention (MQA) [7, 8] derived via ψ\psi-selection, achieving a proven hq/hk​vh_{q}/h_{kv} reduction in KV traffic. All programs are verified against PyTorch scaled_dot_product_attention.

1 Introduction

1.1 Background

The Mathematics of Arrays (MoA) [3] is a formal algebra of multi-dimensional arrays whose primitive operations — ψ\psi-selection, ρ\rho (shape), ι\iota (index generation), γ\gamma (linear offset), and the Omega (Ω\Omega) family of inner products — compose provably minimal computations. The Denotational Normal Form (DNF) specifies what to compute; the Operational Normal Form (ONF) specifies how to lay it out in memory. The companion paper [1] applies MoA to the forward training pass of transformer attention [6], deriving the DNF and proving via the Storage Theorem (Theorem 2.7 of [1]) that the resulting ONF achieves the information-theoretic minimum DRAM traffic. The HAL companion [2] extends this to the backward pass and fused kernel.

1.2 Contributions

This paper shows that the same DNF, with the query-row index i′i^{\prime} fixed to the current decode step, yields four inference artifacts.

  1. 1.

    Decode DNF (§2): the ψ\psi-reduction eliminates the K⊤K^{\top} buffer implicit in the standard formula A=softmax⁡(Q​K⊤/dk)A=\mathrm{softmax}(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{k}}), reducing the score computation to s→=𝑠𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑒(q→(+.×Ω⟨1,2⟩)K)\vec{s}=\mathit{scale}\,(\vec{q}\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle})\;K) with KK accessed row-by-row in its natural layout. Memory traffic: MMoAdec=(dk+n​dk+n​dv+dv)×4​BM^{\mathrm{dec}}_{\mathrm{MoA}}=(d_{k}+nd_{k}+nd_{v}+d_{v})\times 4\,\mathrm{B}, is then proven minimal by Storage Theorem 2.7 of [1].

  2. 2.

    C/OpenACC GPU kernel (§4): ONF γ\gamma stride arithmetic gives coalesced memory access; the coalescing criterion is stated as a γ\gamma-difference condition.

  3. 3.

    KV-cache accumulation (§5): MoA concatenation #\# appends one row per step at the pre-computed γ\gamma offset, with proven O⁡(dk+dv)O(d_{k}+d_{v}) per-step traffic.

  4. 4.

    GQA/MQA (§6): ψ\psi-selection ⟨gk​v⟩​ψ​K\langle g_{kv}\rangle\psi\,K maps each query head to its KV group without materialising the broadcast, reducing traffic by hq/hk​vh_{q}/h_{kv}.

1.3 Notation and Terminology

Figure 1 summarises the relationship between the three companion papers and the importance of memory minimality at every stage.

A transformer [6] is a neural network in which each output element is a learned weighted combination of all input elements (attention). A token is the basic unit of text processed by the model (typically a word or sub-word). Autoregressive inference generates output one token at a time, feeding each generated token back as input; at each step a single query vector q→=WQ​x→\vec{q}=W_{Q}\vec{x} is produced from the current token embedding x→\vec{x} via learned projection WQW_{Q}. All past key vectors k→l=WK​x→l\vec{k}_{l}=W_{K}\vec{x}_{l} and value vectors v→l=WV​x→l\vec{v}_{l}=W_{V}\vec{x}_{l} are accumulated in the KV cache: KK (shape, ρ⁡(K)=⟨n,dk⟩\rho(K)=\langle n,d_{k}\rangle) and VV (shape, ρ⁡(V)=⟨n,dv⟩\rho(V)=\langle n,d_{v}\rangle), where nn grows by one per step. The dominant cost at each step is reading the full KV cache from DRAM: O⁡(n​dk+n​dv)O(nd_{k}+nd_{v}) bytes, unavoidable by any correct implementation (Storage Theorem 2.7 of [1]). MoA proves this bound algebraically before code is written.

MoA notation used throughout: ρ⁡(A)\rho(A) denotes the shape of array AA; ⟨i0,…,ir−1⟩​ψ​A\langle i_{0},\ldots,i_{r-1}\rangle\psi\,A selects element (i0,…,ir−1)(i_{0},\ldots,i_{r-1}); γ⁡(⟨i0,…⟩,ρ⁡(A))\gamma(\langle i_{0},\ldots\rangle,\rho(A)) is the linear memory offset; A(+.×Ω⟨σl,σr⟩)BA\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle\sigma_{l},\sigma_{r}\rangle})\;B is the Omega inner product with left rank σl\sigma_{l}, right rank σr\sigma_{r}; A​#​BA\;\#\;B concatenates along the leading axis. All multiplication uses ×\times.

2 Decode DNF

Formal Inputs

At decode step tt with nn cached tokens:

  • •

    q→\vec{q}: ρ⁡(q→)=⟨dk⟩\rho(\vec{q})=\langle d_{k}\rangle — query vector for the current token.

  • •

    KK: ρ⁡(K)=⟨n,dk⟩\rho(K)=\langle n,d_{k}\rangle — nn rows, each row ⟨l⟩​ψ​K\langle l\rangle\psi\,K (shape ⟨dk⟩\langle d_{k}\rangle) is the key vector for cached token ll. K⊤K^{\top} would have shape ⟨dk,n⟩\langle d_{k},n\rangle; the ψ\psi-reduction accesses rows of KK directly so K⊤K^{\top} is never computed thus saving transfers and storage.

  • •

    VV: ρ⁡(V)=⟨n,dv⟩\rho(V)=\langle n,d_{v}\rangle — nn rows, each row ⟨l⟩​ψ​V\langle l\rangle\psi\,V (shape ⟨dv⟩\langle d_{v}\rangle) is the value vector for cached token ll.

Output: 𝑜𝑢𝑡→\vec{\mathit{out}}, ρ⁡(𝑜𝑢𝑡→)=⟨dv⟩\rho(\vec{\mathit{out}})=\langle d_{v}\rangle; its dd-th element is ⟨d⟩​ψ​𝑜𝑢𝑡→\langle d\rangle\psi\,\vec{\mathit{out}}.

An attention head is an independent copy of the attention computation with its own learned key, query, and value projections. Using hh heads in parallel (multi-head attention) allows the model to extract different types of relationships from the input simultaneously [6]. In the multi-head case KK becomes rank-3 (ρ⁡(K)=⟨h,n,dk⟩\rho(K)=\langle h,n,d_{k}\rangle) or rank-4 (ρ⁡(K)=⟨B,h,n,dk⟩\rho(K)=\langle B,h,n,d_{k}\rangle), where batch BB is the number of independent sequences processed simultaneously.

The Omega operator Ω⟨1,2⟩\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle} generalizes automatically: σl=1\sigma_{l}=1 uses a rank-1 vector ; σr=2\sigma_{r}=2 uses a rank-2 matrix as l/r arguments. Leading batch or head dimensions are outer indices iterated over by Omega — no re-derivation is needed. How K⊤K^{\top} is eliminated by ψ\psi-reduction. The standard attention formula contains K⊤K^{\top}:

A\displaystyle A =softmax⁡(Q​K⊤/dk),\displaystyle=\mathrm{softmax}(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{k}}),
Q,K:ρ=⟨n,dk⟩,Q​K⊤:ρ=⟨n,n⟩.\displaystyle Q,K:\rho=\langle n,d_{k}\rangle,\quad QK^{\top}:\rho=\langle n,n\rangle.

The arXiv paper [1] starts from this formula and applies the ψ\psi-reduction. The key step: instead of forming Q​K⊤QK^{\top} (which requires materialising K⊤K^{\top} in memory), the ψ\psi-reduction shows that each element can be computed by accessing KK directly:

⟨i′,l⟩ψ(QK⊤)=⟨i′⟩ψQ(+.×Ω⟨1,1⟩)⟨l⟩ψK.\langle i^{\prime},l\rangle\psi\,(QK^{\top})=\langle i^{\prime}\rangle\psi\,Q\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 1,1\rangle})\;\langle l\rangle\psi\,K.

where this specific Ω\Omega expression implements the product. The columns of K⊤K^{\top} are exactly the rows ⟨l⟩​ψ​K\langle l\rangle\psi\,K of KK — so K⊤K^{\top} is algebraically present in the starting formula but the ψ\psi-reduction proves it never needs to be materialised. The Storage Theorem (Theorem 2.7 of [1]) then guarantees this is the minimum-traffic access pattern.

For the decode case (this paper), QQ reduces to a single query vector q→\vec{q}, so the ψ\psi-reduction over i′i^{\prime} disappears (there is only one query row), giving directly:

s→[l]=𝑠𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑒q→(+.×Ω⟨1,1⟩)⟨l⟩ψK.\vec{s}[l]=\mathit{scale}\;\vec{q}\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 1,1\rangle})\;\langle l\rangle\psi\,K.

K⊤K^{\top} was in the original formulation; the ψ\psi-reduction removed the need to materialise it before any code is written. This is the central result of [1] applied to the decode setting.

This is equations (4)–(6) of [1] with the query-row index i′i^{\prime} fixed to the current token: eq. (4) is the score ψ\psi-reduction, eq. (5) the softmax, eq. (6) the weighted sum. No new Omega derivation is required. Independence of q→\vec{q} and KK. q→\vec{q} and KK are produced independently:

  • •

    q→=WQ​x→current\vec{q}=W_{Q}\vec{x}_{\mathrm{current}} is the projection of the current token embedding through the learned query matrix WQW_{Q}, ρ⁡(WQ)=⟨dk,d⟩\rho(W_{Q})=\langle d_{k},d\rangle.

  • •

    ⟨l⟩​ψ​K=WK​x→l\langle l\rangle\psi\,K=W_{K}\vec{x}_{l} is the projection of the ll-th past token embedding through the learned key matrix WKW_{K}, stored as row ll of the KV cache.

Neither q→\vec{q} nor KK is derived from the other. Step I asks: how similar is my current query q→\vec{q} to each of the nn stored key vectors ⟨l⟩​ψ​K\langle l\rangle\psi\,K?

Step I – Scores. The ψ\psi-reduction selects row ll of KK as ⟨l⟩​ψ​K\langle l\rangle\psi\,K (shape ⟨dk⟩\langle d_{k}\rangle) and contracts it with q→\vec{q} via the inner product:

Remark 1.

The standard formula Q​K⊤QK^{\top} is algebraically present as the starting point (see §2 preamble); the ψ\psi-reduction proves K⊤K^{\top} need never be materialised. In MoA there are no column vectors: q→\vec{q} and KK are both rank-≥1\geq 1 arrays and contraction is expressed directly via Ω⟨1,2⟩\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle}.

s→​[l]\displaystyle\vec{s}[l] =𝑠𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑒(q→(+.×Ω⟨1,1⟩)⟨l⟩ψK)\displaystyle=\mathit{scale}\;\bigl(\vec{q}\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 1,1\rangle})\;\langle l\rangle\psi\,K\bigr)
=𝑠𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑒​∑j=0dk−1⟨j⟩​ψ​q→×⟨l,j⟩​ψ​K.\displaystyle=\mathit{scale}\textstyle\sum_{j=0}^{d_{k}-1}\langle j\rangle\psi\,\vec{q}\times\langle l,j\rangle\psi\,K.

Over all nn rows simultaneously, with σl=1\sigma_{l}=1 exposing q→\vec{q} as a whole rank-1 vector and σr=2\sigma_{r}=2 exposing KK (shape ⟨n,dk⟩\langle n,d_{k}\rangle) as a whole rank-2 array, the Omega expression is:

s→\displaystyle\vec{s} =𝑠𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑒(q→(+.×Ω⟨1,2⟩)K),ρ(s→)=⟨n⟩.\displaystyle=\mathit{scale}\;\bigl(\vec{q}\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle})\;K\bigr),\quad\rho(\vec{s})=\langle n\rangle. (1)

This equals 𝑠𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑒​K​q→\mathit{scale}\,K\vec{q} (matrix-vector product with KK in its natural row-major layout). No transpose is formed: the Cartesian coordinate interchange is implicit in the ψ\psi-reduction, which reads KK row by row as stored. The Python equivalent is scale*(K@q), not scale*(q@K.T). Ω⟨1,2⟩\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle} is fixed: it always pairs one rank-1 vector from the left with one rank-2 matrix from the right, applying +.×+.\times to produce a scalar for each pair. As the rank of the arguments grows, the same partitioning lifts naturally — superscripts denote rank, Ω⟨1,2⟩\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle} never changes, only the result rank grows:

  • •

    q1→(+.×Ω⟨1,2⟩)K2→s1→\vec{q^{1}}\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle})\;K^{2}\to\vec{s^{1}} (vector-matrix product)

  • •

    A2(+.×Ω⟨1,2⟩)K3→A^{2}\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle})\;K^{3}\to rank-2 (each row of AA with each matrix of KK)

  • •

    A3(+.×Ω⟨1,2⟩)K4→A^{3}\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle})\;K^{4}\to rank-3 (same, one rank higher)

This is how MoA handles batched and multi-head attention without re-derivation. No K⊤K^{\top} buffer is formed; KK is read once and fully consumed in Step I.

Step II – Numerically stable softmax. KK does not appear in Step II at all. By the time Step II runs, KK has already been fully processed and discarded. Step II operates only on the rank-1 score vector s→\vec{s} (shape ⟨n⟩\langle n\rangle) produced by Step I — no matrix, no K⊤K^{\top}, no KK. In the standard training formula, softmax would be applied to the full n×nn\times n score matrix Q​K⊤/dkQK^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{k}} and its Jacobian would be n×nn\times n. Here, softmax operates on a single rank-1 vector s→\vec{s} and the MoA ψ\psi-reduction eliminates all intermediates: s→\vec{s}, e→\vec{e}, a→\vec{a} and scalars mm, ZZ are O⁡(n)O(n) on-stack and never written to DRAM.

m\displaystyle m =maxl⁡s→​[l],\displaystyle=\max_{l}\vec{s}[l],
e→​[l]\displaystyle\vec{e}[l] =exp⁡(s→​[l]−m),\displaystyle=\exp(\vec{s}[l]-m),
Z\displaystyle Z =∑l′=0n−1e→​[l′],\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{l^{\prime}=0}^{n-1}\vec{e}[l^{\prime}],
a→​[l]\displaystyle\vec{a}[l] =e→​[l]/Z,0≤l<n.\displaystyle=\vec{e}[l]/Z,\quad 0\leq l<n. (2)

No n×nn\times n score matrix or Jacobian is allocated.

Numerical stability: subtracting m=maxl⁡s→​[l]m=\max_{l}\vec{s}[l] before exponentiating does not change the softmax value (the mm terms cancel) but prevents overflow. 𝑠𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑒=1/dk\mathit{scale}=1/\sqrt{d_{k}} normalises variance to 1 for random unit-norm inputs.

Step III – Weighted sum:

⟨d⟩​ψ​𝑜𝑢𝑡→\displaystyle\langle d\rangle\psi\,\vec{\mathit{out}} =∑l=0n−1⟨l⟩​ψ​a→×⟨l,d⟩​ψ​V,\displaystyle=\textstyle\sum_{l=0}^{n-1}\langle l\rangle\psi\,\vec{a}\times\langle l,d\rangle\psi\,V,
0≤d<dv, 0≤l<n.\displaystyle\hskip 40.00006pt0\leq d<d_{v},\;0\leq l<n. (3)

VV is read once in row-major order; no intermediate array exists. Concrete example (n=2n=2, dk=2d_{k}=2, dv=2d_{v}=2, 𝑠𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑒=1/2\mathit{scale}=1/\sqrt{2}). Let

  • •

    Step I: let qj=⟨j⟩​ψ​q→q_{j}=\langle j\rangle\psi\,\vec{q}, Kl​j=⟨l,j⟩​ψ​KK_{lj}=\langle l,j\rangle\psi\,K.

    s→​[0]\displaystyle\vec{s}[0] =𝑠𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑒⁡(q0​K00+q1​K01)=12​(1+0)=12,\displaystyle=\mathit{scale}(q_{0}K_{00}+q_{1}K_{01})=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1+0)=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}},

Proposition 1 (Decode memory minimality).

The decode DNF achieves MMoAdec=(dk+n​dk+n​dv+dv)×4​B=O⁡(n​dk+n​dv)M^{\mathrm{dec}}_{\mathrm{MoA}}=(d_{k}+nd_{k}+nd_{v}+d_{v})\times 4\,\mathrm{B}=O(nd_{k}+nd_{v}) memory usage..

3 Python Implementation

Standard PyTorch Reference

Two PyTorch shape operations appear throughout: .unsqueeze(d) inserts a new size-1 dimension at position dd (e.g. ⟨dk⟩→⟨1,dk⟩\langle d_{k}\rangle\to\langle 1,d_{k}\rangle); .squeeze() removes all size-1 dimensions (e.g. ⟨1,1,1,dv⟩→⟨dv⟩\langle 1,1,1,d_{v}\rangle\to\langle d_{v}\rangle), recovering a MoA rank-1 vector.

The conventional single-query decode in PyTorch unsqueezes q→\vec{q} to shape ⟨1,dk⟩\langle 1,d_{k}\rangle, forms the score row via q_ @ K.T (note: .T creates a transposed view; MoA avoids this entirely), applies softmax, and squeezes the result:

The MoA version (below) replaces q_ @ K.T with q→(+.×Ω⟨1,2⟩)K\vec{q}\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle})\;K: the ψ\psi-reduction reads KK row by row in its natural layout — no transposed view is created — and the Storage Theorem proves the result is memory-minimal by construction.

MoA - Based Implementation

moa_decode.py mirrors the three DNF steps directly. The MoA formulation:

  • •

    Step I (scores, eq. (1)):

    s→=𝑠𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑒(q→(+.×Ω⟨1,2⟩)K),ρ(s→)=⟨n⟩.\vec{s}=\mathit{scale}\;\bigl(\vec{q}\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle})\;K\bigr),\quad\rho(\vec{s})=\langle n\rangle.
  • •

    Step II (softmax, eq. (2)):

    a→​[l]=e→​[l]/∑l′=0n−1e→​[l′],ρ⁡(a→)=⟨n⟩.\vec{a}[l]=\vec{e}[l]\big/\textstyle\sum_{l^{\prime}=0}^{n-1}\vec{e}[l^{\prime}],\quad\rho(\vec{a})=\langle n\rangle.
  • •

    Step III (weighted sum, eq. (3)):

    𝑜𝑢𝑡→=a→(+.×Ω⟨1,2⟩)V,ρ(𝑜𝑢𝑡→)=⟨dv⟩.\vec{\mathit{out}}=\vec{a}\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle})\;V,\quad\rho(\vec{\mathit{out}})=\langle d_{v}\rangle.

Each listing block below corresponds to one step.

Reference Implementation

PyTorch — a widely-used open-source numerical computing library for neural networks (A. Paszke et al., NeurIPS 2019) — provides scaled_dot_product_attention (SDPA) as a numerically verified fused reference implementation of the attention operation. In the full training setting SDPA computes softmax(𝑠𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑒Q(+.×Ω⟨2,2⟩)K)(+.×Ω⟨2,2⟩)V\mathrm{softmax}(\mathit{scale}\;Q\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 2,2\rangle})\;K)\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 2,2\rangle})\;V where ρ⁡(Q)=⟨n,dk⟩\rho(Q)=\langle n,d_{k}\rangle and the output has shape ⟨n,dv⟩\langle n,d_{v}\rangle. Here Ω⟨2,2⟩\Omega_{\langle 2,2\rangle} has σl=σr=2\sigma_{l}=\sigma_{r}=2 (both arguments rank-2); for the single decode step, QQ reduces to rank-1 q→\vec{q} so Ω⟨1,2⟩\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle} is used throughout this paper. For a single decode step there is only one query vector q→∈ℝdk\vec{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}, ρ⁡(q→)=⟨dk⟩\rho(\vec{q})=\langle d_{k}\rangle. In MoA there are no row or column vectors: the score vector s→\vec{s}, weight vector a→\vec{a}, and output 𝑜𝑢𝑡→\vec{\mathit{out}} are all rank-1 arrays. The decode computation proceeds in three steps, each expressed as a ψ\psi-reduction that eliminates intermediates:

  • •

    Step I (scores, ψ\psi-reduction over KK): q→(+.×Ω⟨1,2⟩)K∈ℝn\vec{q}\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle})\;K\in\mathbb{R}^{n} — no K⊤K^{\top} buffer.

  • •

    Step II (softmax, ψ\psi-reduction over s→\vec{s}): softmax⁡(s→/dk)∈ℝn\mathrm{softmax}(\vec{s}/\sqrt{d_{k}})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} — no n×nn\times n Jacobian.

  • •

    Step III (weighted sum, ψ\psi-reduction over VV): a→(+.×Ω⟨1,2⟩)V∈ℝdv\vec{a}\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle})\;V\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} (=𝑜𝑢𝑡→=\vec{\mathit{out}}).

Every intermediate and output is a rank-1 vector in MoA: s→,a→∈ℝn\vec{s},\vec{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and 𝑜𝑢𝑡→∈ℝdv\vec{\mathit{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}. This is exactly what the decode DNF computes in equations (1)–(3): s→\vec{s} is the score vector, a→\vec{a} is the weight vector, and 𝑜𝑢𝑡→\vec{\mathit{out}} is the rank-1 output vector. SDPA is PyTorch’s own numerically verified fused kernel, making it a valid ground truth. Note: PyTorch’s SDPA requires (B, H, S, D) input shape (batch, heads, sequence, dimension), so dummy size-1 dimensions must be added before the call and removed with .squeeze() afterwards (defined above). To call it as a reference, q→\vec{q}, KK, VV are wrapped with dummy batch B=1B=1 and head H=1H=1 dimensions to match the required (B, H, S, D) input shape:

⬇
1 ## Single decode step: vq:(dk,) K:(n,dk) V:(n,dv)
2 q_ = vq.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0)
3 ## -> (1, 1, 1, dk)
4 k_ = K.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # -> (1, 1, n, dk)
5 v_ = V.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # -> (1, 1, n, dv)
6 ## SDPA output: (1, 1, 1, dv) -> squeeze -> (dv,)
7 out_ref = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(
8 q_, k_, v_, scale=scale).squeeze()

The .squeeze() removes all size-1 dimensions, giving 𝑜𝑢𝑡→ref∈ℝdv\vec{\mathit{out}}_{\mathrm{ref}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} for direct comparison with moa_decode output. Table 1 reports the verification. Errors are float32 round-off only, an order of magnitude smaller than the training kernel (9×10−59\times 10^{-5}) because the decode path has no backward accumulation.

4 C/OpenACC Kernel

4.1 ONF Stride Arithmetic

Applying the γ\gamma primitive (Definition 2.1 of [1]) to row-major storage:

γ⁡(⟨l,j⟩,⟨n,dk⟩)=l×dk+j(K​ offset),\gamma(\langle l,j\rangle,\langle n,d_{k}\rangle)=l\times d_{k}+j\quad(K\text{ offset}),
γ⁡(⟨l,d⟩,⟨n,dv⟩)=l×dv+d(V​ offset).\gamma(\langle l,d\rangle,\langle n,d_{v}\rangle)=l\times d_{v}+d\quad(V\text{ offset}).

These stride expressions appear verbatim as K[l*dk+j] and V[l*dv+d] in Listing 3. Concrete example (n=3n=3, dk=2d_{k}=2, dv=2d_{v}=2). The six elements of KK (shape ⟨3,2⟩\langle 3,2\rangle, row-major) lie at flat offsets:

⟨0,0⟩:γ⁡(⟨0,0⟩,⟨3,2⟩)=0×2+0=0⟨0,1⟩:0×2+1=1⟨1,0⟩:1×2+0=2⟨1,1⟩:1×2+1=3⟨2,0⟩:2×2+0=4⟨2,1⟩:2×2+1=5\begin{array}[]{ll}\langle 0,0\rangle:&\gamma(\langle 0,0\rangle,\langle 3,2\rangle)=0\times 2+0=0\\ \langle 0,1\rangle:&0\times 2+1=1\\ \langle 1,0\rangle:&1\times 2+0=2\\ \langle 1,1\rangle:&1\times 2+1=3\\ \langle 2,0\rangle:&2\times 2+0=4\\ \langle 2,1\rangle:&2\times 2+1=5\end{array}

So K[l*2+j] in C accesses ⟨l,j⟩​ψ​K\langle l,j\rangle\psi\,K directly – no transpose buffer is needed.

4.2 Dimension Lifting and Hardware-Coalescing Proof

Dimension lifting maps a flat index space ⟨N⟩\langle N\rangle to a structured processing array ⟨Π,⌈N/Π⌉⟩\langle\Pi,\lceil N/\Pi\rceil\rangle, partitioning work across hierarchical execution blocks. In modern streaming multiprocessors (GPUs), memory throughput is governed strictly by hardware coalescing: global memory requests across a warp — a group of 32 threads that execute in lock-step on a GPU streaming multiprocessor — are merged if those threads access contiguous memory locations.

Let the core evaluation of Step III map an abstract 2-D sequence-to-feature reduction domain D=⟨n⟩×⟨dv⟩D=\langle n\rangle\times\langle d_{v}\rangle. In parallel architectures, an MoA compiler solves layout compatibility by formalizing a hardware mapping tree. We define multi-level lifting primitives:

⟨n⟩\displaystyle\langle n\rangle ↦⟨Πg,⌈n/Πg⌉⟩(Sequence Rows),\displaystyle\;\mapsto\;\langle\Pi_{g},\,\lceil n/\Pi_{g}\rceil\rangle\quad\text{(Sequence Rows)}, (4)
⟨dv⟩\displaystyle\langle d_{v}\rangle ↦⟨Πv,⌈dv/Πv⌉⟩(Feature Columns).\displaystyle\;\mapsto\;\langle\Pi_{v},\,\lceil d_{v}/\Pi_{v}\rceil\rangle\quad\text{(Feature Columns)}. (5)

The combined domain is reshaped via ρ\rho to mirror the GPU topology:

S=⟨Πg,⌈n/Πg⌉,Πv,⌈dv/Πv⌉⟩,S=\langle\Pi_{g},\lceil n/\Pi_{g}\rceil,\Pi_{v},\lceil d_{v}/\Pi_{v}\rceil\rangle,

A coordinate index vector in this space is I=⟨g,i,v,j⟩I=\langle g,i,v,j\rangle, where gg is the gang, ii is sequential work inside the block, vv is the vector thread (warp channel), and jj is the register stride.

To detect memory bottlenecks, the compiler evaluates the γ\gamma stride between adjacent vector threads vv and v+1v+1 for a fixed (g,i,j)(g,i,j). Under row-major layout with the hardware-to-logical mapping l=g⁡⌈n/Πg⌉+il=g\lceil n/\Pi_{g}\rceil+i, d=v⁡⌈dv/Πv⌉+jd=v\lceil d_{v}/\Pi_{v}\rceil+j:

γ⁡(⟨g,i,v,j⟩,S)=(g⁡⌈n/Πg⌉+i)×dv+v⁡⌈dv/Πv⌉+j.\gamma(\langle g,i,v,j\rangle,S)=\bigl(g\lceil n/\Pi_{g}\rceil+i\bigr)\times d_{v}+v\lceil d_{v}/\Pi_{v}\rceil+j.

The adjacent-thread γ\gamma difference is:

γ⁡(⟨g,i,v+1,j⟩,S)−γ⁡(⟨g,i,v,j⟩,S)=⌈dv/Πv⌉.\gamma(\langle g,i,v+1,j\rangle,S)-\gamma(\langle g,i,v,j\rangle,S)=\lceil d_{v}/\Pi_{v}\rceil.

Coalescing Criterion (in MoA γ\gamma terms): access is perfectly coalesced if and only if

γ⁡(⟨g,i,v+1,j⟩,S)−γ⁡(⟨g,i,v,j⟩,S)=1,\gamma(\langle g,i,v+1,j\rangle,S)-\gamma(\langle g,i,v,j\rangle,S)=1,

i.e., adjacent vector threads access physically adjacent memory locations (Definition 2.1 of [1]).

In the naive DNF, dd maps to gangs and ll to vectors. The adjacent-thread γ\gamma difference becomes ⌈dv/Πv⌉=dv=64\lceil d_{v}/\Pi_{v}\rceil=d_{v}=64, meaning threads hit data 256 bytes apart — shattering coalescing.

By transposing the execution array (hoisting the dd loop as the inner vectorized axis), the MoA compiler sets Πv=dv\Pi_{v}=d_{v}, so ⌈dv/Πv⌉=1\lceil d_{v}/\Pi_{v}\rceil=1, and the γ\gamma difference equals 1 — aligning threads with contiguous 128-bit cache lines. The transformed, fully coalesced algorithm is implemented in Listing 3; this coalescing strategy follows the GPU energy-efficiency approach of [5]. The column space loop over dd is hoisted as the inner vectorized axis, ensuring maximal memory saturation.

4.3 OpenACC Annotations

Three OpenACC pragma types appear in Listing 3:

  • •

    #pragma acc parallel loop gang distributes the outer loop across GPU gangs (groups of warps).

  • •

    #pragma acc loop vector distributes the inner loop across threads within a gang (the vector lane).

  • •

    #pragma acc atomic ensures that when multiple gangs update the same out[d] element simultaneously (Pass 3, the weighted sum), the read-modify-write is indivisible — preventing a race condition (a data corruption that occurs when two threads read, then both write, the same location without coordination). The reduction clauses in Passes 1 and 2 use a more efficient tree-reduction pattern rather than serialising through a single atomic; Pass 3 requires atomic because each out[d] is accumulated from all nn gang iterations.

4.4 Verification

Compiled with clang -O3 (macOS) or gcc -O3 (Linux) — no flags needed beyond -lm for CPU verification. The #pragma acc directives are silently ignored by plain C compilers; the moa_decode_cpu sequential reference runs in the same binary.

The CPU kernel matches the sequential reference to ‖err‖∞=0\|\mathrm{err}\|_{\infty}=0 (exact IEEE-754 equality for the same operation order). For GPU execution: replace clang with nvc -acc=gpu -gpu=cc120 (NVIDIA B200), clang -fopenacc --offload-arch=gfx942 (AMD MI300X), or icx -fopenacc (Intel Aurora).

5 Multi-Step KV-Cache Accumulation

5.1 Cache Append Expression

At each decode step tt, one new key vector k→t∈ℝdk\vec{k}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}, ρ⁡(k→t)=⟨dk⟩\rho(\vec{k}_{t})=\langle d_{k}\rangle, and value vector v→t∈ℝdv\vec{v}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}, ρ⁡(v→t)=⟨dv⟩\rho(\vec{v}_{t})=\langle d_{v}\rangle, are appended to the caches using MoA concatenation #\# along axis 0, defined as: A​#​b→A\;\#\;\vec{b} appends rank-1 vector b→\vec{b} (shape ⟨dk⟩\langle d_{k}\rangle) as a new final row of rank-2 array AA (shape ⟨t,dk⟩\langle t,d_{k}\rangle), giving ρ⁡(A​#​b→)=⟨t+1,dk⟩\rho(A\;\#\;\vec{b})=\langle t+1,d_{k}\rangle without copying any existing data:

Kt+1\displaystyle K_{t+1} =Kt​#​k→t,\displaystyle=K_{t}\;\#\;\vec{k}_{t}, (6)
Vt+1\displaystyle V_{t+1} =Vt​#​v→t.\displaystyle=V_{t}\;\#\;\vec{v}_{t}. (7)

In MoA there are no row or column vectors, so no reshape is needed: #\# appends k→t\vec{k}_{t} (shape ⟨dk⟩\langle d_{k}\rangle) as a new final row of KtK_{t} (shape ⟨t,dk⟩\langle t,d_{k}\rangle), giving ρ⁡(Kt+1)=⟨t+1,dk⟩\rho(K_{t+1})=\langle t+1,d_{k}\rangle. The trailing dimension dkd_{k} matches, so #\# is well-defined without Omega lifting. Omega would be needed only if #\# were being lifted over a batch of such pairs. Concrete example (t=2t=2, dk=3d_{k}=3). Let ki​j≡⟨i,j⟩​ψ​K2k_{ij}\equiv\langle i,j\rangle\psi\,K_{2}. K2K_{2} has shape ⟨2,3⟩\langle 2,3\rangle; k→2=⟨a,b,c⟩\vec{k}_{2}=\langle a,b,c\rangle has shape ⟨3⟩\langle 3\rangle:

K2=(k00k01k02k10k11k12),ρ⁡(K2)=⟨2,3⟩.K_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}k_{00}&k_{01}&k_{02}\\ k_{10}&k_{11}&k_{12}\end{pmatrix},\quad\rho(K_{2})=\langle 2,3\rangle.

K3≡K2​#​k→2K_{3}\equiv K_{2}\;\#\;\vec{k}_{2} is defined as the result of appending k→2\vec{k}_{2} as the new final row of K2K_{2}:

K3=K2​#​k→2=(k00k01k02k10k11k12abc).K_{3}=K_{2}\;\#\;\vec{k}_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}k_{00}&k_{01}&k_{02}\\ k_{10}&k_{11}&k_{12}\\ a&b&c\end{pmatrix}.

ρ⁡(K3)=⟨3,3⟩\rho(K_{3})=\langle 3,3\rangle. In the ONF, the new row is written at the gamma offset γ⁡(⟨t,j⟩,⟨T,dk⟩)=t×dk+j\gamma(\langle t,j\rangle,\langle T,d_{k}\rangle)=t\times d_{k}+j, so elements aa, bb, cc land at offsets 2×3+0=62\times 3+0=6, 77, 88 in the flat array. No existing data is moved.

Proposition 2 (Cache-append traffic).

Equations (6)–(7) append k→t\vec{k}_{t} and v→t\vec{v}_{t} directly, moving exactly (dk+dv)×4​B(d_{k}+d_{v})\times 4\,\,\mathrm{B} per step, independent of tt. This is the information-theoretic minimum: one key row and one value row must be written regardless of algorithm.

5.2 Combined Per-Step Cost

The total traffic at step tt is:

Mstep​(t)\displaystyle M_{\mathrm{step}}(t) =(dk+dv)×4⏟append ​O​(dk+dv)+(t​dk+t​dv)×4⏟decode ​O​(t​dk+t​dv).\displaystyle=\underbrace{(d_{k}+d_{v})\times 4}_{\text{append }O(d_{k}+d_{v})}+\underbrace{(td_{k}+td_{v})\times 4}_{\text{decode }O(td_{k}+td_{v})}. (8)

Summed over TT output tokens:

Mtotal=∑t=1TMstep​(t)=O⁡(T2​(dk+dv)).M_{\mathrm{total}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}M_{\mathrm{step}}(t)=O\!\left(T^{2}(d_{k}+d_{v})\right).

This quadratic growth in TT is unavoidable (every token must attend over all previous tokens), but MoA makes the constant factor minimal and the bound a theorem.

6 Grouped-Query and Multi-Query Attention

6.1 Psi-Selection Expression

In GQA, hqh_{q} query heads share hk​v<hqh_{kv}<h_{q} KV heads (hk​vh_{kv} divides hqh_{q}), with KK of shape ⟨hk​v,n,dk⟩\langle h_{kv},n,d_{k}\rangle. The scalar elements of KK are defined by ψ\psi-selection with a full index vector:

⟨g,i,j⟩​ψ​K{0≤g<hk​v(KV head)0≤i<n(sequence position)0≤j<dk(feature)\langle g,i,j\rangle\,\psi\,K\quad\begin{cases}0\leq g<h_{kv}&\text{(KV head)}\\ 0\leq i<n&\text{(sequence position)}\\ 0\leq j<d_{k}&\text{(feature)}\end{cases} (9)

A partial index vector ⟨gk​v⟩\langle g_{kv}\rangle selects the entire gk​vg_{kv}-th KV head slab:

Kg=⟨gk​v⟩​ψ​K,ρ⁡(Kg)=⟨n,dk⟩,K_{g}=\langle g_{kv}\rangle\,\psi\,K,\quad\rho(K_{g})=\langle n,d_{k}\rangle, (10)

whose elements satisfy ⟨i,j⟩​ψ​(⟨gk​v⟩​ψ​K)=⟨gk​v,i,j⟩​ψ​K\langle i,j\rangle\,\psi\,(\langle g_{kv}\rangle\,\psi\,K)=\langle g_{kv},i,j\rangle\,\psi\,K. The group assignment for query head gg is gk​v=⌊g×hk​v/hq⌋g_{kv}=\lfloor g\times h_{kv}/h_{q}\rfloor. This drops the leading head dimension, leaving a 2-D array of shape ⟨n,dk⟩\langle n,d_{k}\rangle passed directly to the decode DNF (equation (1)). No Omega lifting is needed and no expanded ⟨hq,n,dk⟩\langle h_{q},n,d_{k}\rangle tensor is materialized. Concrete example (hq=4h_{q}=4, hk​v=2h_{kv}=2, n=3n=3, dk=2d_{k}=2, 𝑔𝑟𝑜𝑢𝑝​_​𝑠𝑖𝑧𝑒=2\mathit{group\_size}=2). KK has shape ⟨2,3,2⟩\langle 2,3,2\rangle with elements ⟨g,i,j⟩​ψ​K\langle g,i,j\rangle\,\psi\,K. The two KV slabs (each shape ⟨3,2⟩\langle 3,2\rangle) are:

⟨0⟩​ψ​K=(⟨0,0,0⟩​ψ​K⟨0,0,1⟩​ψ​K⟨0,1,0⟩​ψ​K⟨0,1,1⟩​ψ​K⟨0,2,0⟩​ψ​K⟨0,2,1⟩​ψ​K)\langle 0\rangle\,\psi\,K=\begin{pmatrix}\langle 0,0,0\rangle\,\psi\,K&\langle 0,0,1\rangle\,\psi\,K\\ \langle 0,1,0\rangle\,\psi\,K&\langle 0,1,1\rangle\,\psi\,K\\ \langle 0,2,0\rangle\,\psi\,K&\langle 0,2,1\rangle\,\psi\,K\end{pmatrix}
⟨1⟩​ψ​K=(⟨1,0,0⟩​ψ​K⟨1,0,1⟩​ψ​K⟨1,1,0⟩​ψ​K⟨1,1,1⟩​ψ​K⟨1,2,0⟩​ψ​K⟨1,2,1⟩​ψ​K)\langle 1\rangle\,\psi\,K=\begin{pmatrix}\langle 1,0,0\rangle\,\psi\,K&\langle 1,0,1\rangle\,\psi\,K\\ \langle 1,1,0\rangle\,\psi\,K&\langle 1,1,1\rangle\,\psi\,K\\ \langle 1,2,0\rangle\,\psi\,K&\langle 1,2,1\rangle\,\psi\,K\end{pmatrix}

The four query heads select slabs as follows:

g=0:\displaystyle g=0: gk​v=0,⟨0⟩​ψ​K,ρ=⟨3,2⟩\displaystyle\;g_{kv}=0,\quad\langle 0\rangle\,\psi\,K,\;\rho=\langle 3,2\rangle
g=1:\displaystyle g=1: gk​v=0,⟨0⟩​ψ​K(same slab as g=0)\displaystyle\;g_{kv}=0,\quad\langle 0\rangle\,\psi\,K\quad\text{(same slab as $g=0$)}
g=2:\displaystyle g=2: gk​v=1,⟨1⟩​ψ​K,ρ=⟨3,2⟩\displaystyle\;g_{kv}=1,\quad\langle 1\rangle\,\psi\,K,\;\rho=\langle 3,2\rangle
g=3:\displaystyle g=3: gk​v=1,⟨1⟩​ψ​K(same slab as g=2)\displaystyle\;g_{kv}=1,\quad\langle 1\rangle\,\psi\,K\quad\text{(same slab as $g=2$)}

Query heads 0 and 1 both evaluate ⟨0⟩​ψ​K\langle 0\rangle\,\psi\,K; heads 2 and 3 both evaluate ⟨1⟩​ψ​K\langle 1\rangle\,\psi\,K. By the Storage Theorem, each slab need only be read from DRAM once, giving the hq/hk​v=2×h_{q}/h_{kv}=2\times KV traffic reduction algebraically.

6.2 Dimension Lifting

Dimension lifting is MoA’s way of mapping to the abstract shape of the target architecture. Starting with the ONF shape, each component of the shape is partitioned one or more times to conform to each architectural target, e.g. processors, memory, etc. For example, The qq-head axis and k​vkv-head axis are lifted independently using the dimension-lifting map N↦⟨Π,⌈N/Π⌉⟩N\mapsto\langle\Pi,\lceil N/\Pi\rceil\rangle of Section 2.5 of [1]:

⟨hq⟩\displaystyle\langle h_{q}\rangle ↦⟨Πq,⌈hq/Πq⌉⟩(q-head gang axis),\displaystyle\mapsto\langle\Pi_{q},\lceil h_{q}/\Pi_{q}\rceil\rangle\quad\text{($q$-head gang axis)}, (11)
⟨hk​v⟩\displaystyle\langle h_{kv}\rangle ↦⟨Πk​v,⌈hk​v/Πk​v⌉⟩(KV read axis).\displaystyle\mapsto\langle\Pi_{kv},\lceil h_{kv}/\Pi_{kv}\rceil\rangle\quad\text{(KV read axis)}. (12)

With shared-memory caching (⟨gk​v⟩​ψ​K\langle g_{kv}\rangle\,\psi\,K held in L1 for the hq/hk​vh_{q}/h_{kv} gangs sharing it), the KV traffic reduces from hq×n×dkh_{q}\times n\times d_{k} to hk​v×n×dkh_{kv}\times n\times d_{k} bytes – a factor of hq/hk​vh_{q}/h_{kv}. MQA is the special case hk​v=1h_{kv}=1.

Standard PyTorch GQA expands the KV heads to hqh_{q} by repeat_interleave, materialising a full ⟨hq,n,dk⟩\langle h_{q},n,d_{k}\rangle broadcast tensor:

The MoA version replaces repeat_interleave with ψ\psi-selection ⟨gk​v⟩​ψ​K\langle g_{kv}\rangle\psi\,K, reading each KV slab once per group rather than hq/hk​vh_{q}/h_{kv} times, giving a proven hq/hk​vh_{q}/h_{kv} traffic reduction.

The MoA formulation for GQA uses ψ\psi-selection (eq. (10)) to map each query head gg to its KV group, then applies the decode DNF:

gk​v\displaystyle g_{kv} =⌊g×hk​v/hq⌋,0≤g<hq,\displaystyle=\lfloor g\times h_{kv}/h_{q}\rfloor,\quad 0\leq g<h_{q},
Kg\displaystyle K_{g} =⟨gk​v⟩​ψ​K,ρ⁡(Kg)=⟨n,dk⟩,\displaystyle=\langle g_{kv}\rangle\,\psi\,K,\quad\rho(K_{g})=\langle n,d_{k}\rangle,
𝑜𝑢𝑡→g\displaystyle\vec{\mathit{out}}_{g} =a→g(+.×Ω⟨1,2⟩)Vg,ρ(𝑜𝑢𝑡→g)=⟨dv⟩.\displaystyle=\vec{a}_{g}\;(+.\times\Omega_{\langle 1,2\rangle})\;V_{g},\quad\rho(\vec{\mathit{out}}_{g})=\langle d_{v}\rangle.

No ⟨hq,n,dk⟩\langle h_{q},n,d_{k}\rangle tensor is materialized; each query head reads its assigned slab directly:

6.4 Verification and Traffic

The hq/hk​vh_{q}/h_{kv} traffic reduction is exact and follows algebraically from the ψ\psi-selection expression (10): at hk​v=1h_{kv}=1 (MQA), KV traffic falls from 16.78 MB to 0.52 MB (32×32\times) on top of the baseline MoA decode savings.

8 Conclusion

Four MoA inference artifacts have been derived, implemented, and numerically verified, each following directly from the forward-pass DNF of [1]. The decode DNF is eqs. (4)–(6) of that paper with i′i^{\prime} fixed to the current token: eq. (4) score ψ\psi-reduction, eq. (5) softmax, eq. (6) weighted sum. The C/OpenACC kernel applies the γ\gamma ONF stride arithmetic of [1] §7.2; KV-cache append uses plain #\# concatenation; GQA/MQA uses ψ\psi-selection and the dimension-lifting Section 2.5 map of [1]. In every case the memory bound is a theorem (Storage Theorem 2.7 of [1]) before code is written, and the DNF→\toONF→\toC pipeline ports the result to any architecture without re-derivation.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
